lines: Most small businesses don't have a lead problem.
They have a leak.
Someone fills in your contact form on a Tuesday night, and the notification lands in an inbox nobody checks until Thursday.
By then they've asked two other businesses, and one of them answered in five minutes.
You didn't lose that lead to a better offer.
You lost it to a slower reply.
So here's a fix you can build tonight.
One n8n workflow, about ten minutes once your accounts are connected.
Every lead gets seen and answered within a minute, followed up if nobody gets back to them, and you find out if the whole thing ever breaks.
There are three places a lead slips through, and it's worth naming them, because each one gets its own step.
Leak one, nobody sees it.
The form emails a shared inbox, or a spam folder, or the address of someone who left last year.
Leak two, nobody replies fast.
Someone sees it, means to answer properly, and properly turns into tomorrow.
Leak three, nobody follows up.
One reply goes out, the lead doesn't answer, and the conversation just stops.
Nobody decided to drop it. There was just nothing to remind anyone.
And there's a fourth leak that nobody plans for, which is the fix itself breaking quietly.
We'll get to that one last, because it's the one that turns a good workflow into a false sense of security.
Here's the whole thing.
A trigger that catches the form.
A step that tidies the data.
A row in a sheet, so every lead is written down somewhere.
An instant reply to the lead.
An alert to you.
And a wait that checks back the next day.
No code, and nothing you have to host to try it.
Let's build it in order.
Step one, catch the form.
Start with a Webhook node, or n8n's own Form Trigger if you don't have a form yet.
The webhook gives you a web address.
Most form tools and website builders have a setting that sends every submission to an address like that.
Paste it in there, submit a test, and you'll see the lead arrive in n8n.
One thing catches nearly everyone the first time.
The webhook has a test address and a production address.
The test one only listens while you're watching the editor.
Put the production address in your form, and make sure the workflow is switched on, or it hears nothing.
Step two, write it down.
Add an Edit Fields node and tidy what came in.
Trim the spaces and lower-case the email.
Then add three fields of your own. When it arrived, where it came from, and a status, which starts as new.
Then a Google Sheets node, set to append or update a row, matched on the email.
Someone who fills in the form twice is one lead, not two.
And you always have a list of every enquiry, even if a later step goes wrong.
That status column is the most important field in the whole workflow.
Everything later reads it.
Step three, reply in a minute.
A Gmail or email node sends a reply from your real address.
Keep it short and honest.
Thanks, here's what happens next, and when you'll hear from a person.
Then one question that makes your real reply better, like what their timeline is.
Don't dress it up as a personal note you didn't write.
The point isn't to fool anyone.
The point is that they know within a minute they reached a real business, and that's often enough to stop them filling in the next form.
Step four, tell a human.
Send yourself a message where you'll actually see it.
Slack, Telegram, a text, whatever is on your phone. Not another email.
Put the name, what they asked for, and a link to the row in the message, so you can act on it without opening anything else.
If more than one person handles leads, send it to a shared channel, and have whoever takes it reply in the thread.
Then nobody wonders whether somebody else already got it.
Step five, the next day check.
This is the one that plugs leak three.
Add a Wait node set to twenty-four hours.
When it wakes up, look the lead up in the sheet again and read the status.
Then an If node.
If the status still says new, nobody has replied, and you get a second message. This lead has waited a day.
If someone did reply and changed the status, the workflow just ends.
Notice who that reminder goes to.
You, not the lead.
An automatic chaser to someone who hasn't answered is how a helpful business starts to look like a mailing list.
The workflow's job is to make sure a person follows up, not to do it for them.

lines: Which brings us to leak four.
The day this workflow breaks, it won't tell you.
Leads just stop arriving, and a quiet week looks exactly like a broken form.

lines: So build a second, tiny workflow that starts with an Error Trigger and sends you a message.
Then in the lead workflow's settings, choose it as the error workflow.
Now a failure in any step reaches your phone.
The usual causes are boring.
A Google connection that expired, a form field someone renamed, a sheet column someone deleted.
If your Google connection uses an app that's still in testing mode, its sign-in expires after seven days, so publish the app or expect to reconnect every week.
And once a week, fill in your own form.
Thirty seconds.
If the reply and the alert both arrive, the whole chain works.
So that's the fix.
Catch it.
Write it down.
Reply in a minute.
Tell a human.
Check the next day.
And know when it breaks.
None of this brings you a single new lead.
It just stops you losing the ones that already chose you, which is the cheapest growth there is.
Build it tonight, then fill in your own contact form, and see how long it takes you to hear back.

pills: Keep the leads that already chose you
